source.title: Compressed Computation: Dense Circuits in a Toy Model of the Universal-AND Problem

record.file_problem: The text is complete and readable; it contains minor encoding artifacts in a few places.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies compressed computation in a Universal-AND toy task, not feature storage geometry, polysemanticity, or SAE features. Its discussion of superposition and polysemanticity does not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on dense computation circuits, including learned weight patterns and performance on Universal-AND. These are included as related-but-different findings under fits_no_version; they do not measure the representation or behavior named by any claim version. The paper also cites feature-superposition results, which are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study trains one-layer toy MLPs on Universal-AND with monosemantic inputs and outputs. It studies compressed computation: how AND outputs are computed across a narrow set of neurons. It does not measure feature-storage geometry, sparsity-dependent phase transitions, SAE features, LLM representations or feature dimensionality. Its neurons do contribute to many outputs, but this concerns computation circuits, a related but different construct from the polysemanticity of stored features named in V2 and V3. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Training finds a dense Binary Weighted Circuit for Universal-AND rather than the sparse CiS construction. The approximate analysis suggests it beats that construction when s grows slower than sqrt(d)/log² m. The authors argue dense shared computation challenges sparse-circuit assumptions and gives an additional explanation for why features are rarely monosemantic. The appendix offers an alternative reading: Boolean functions can be read out from randomly superposed sparse features.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains toy networks on a Universal-AND computation task; it does not reproduce the original feature-storage experiment or its measurement of superposed feature directions.
record.method_sensitivity: The learned circuit depends on input sparsity: the binary-weighted circuit is reported at reasonable sparsity, while higher sparsity leads to degenerate solutions; the paper says it did not perform a full sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained Universal-AND toy networks learn a dense binary-weighted circuit in which every neuron contributes to every AND output. At higher sparsity (s ≥ 10, d ≤ m) they fall back to degenerate additive or readout-only solutions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In compressed-computation toy tasks, gradient training with weight decay favours dense shared circuits over sparse theoretical constructions, depending on input sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: The author states the model does not form non-overlapping per-AND circuits even when d equals the number of pairs, so a one-neuron-per-output solution would fit. The author attributes this to weight decay favouring spread-out circuits. No figure or number in the text isolates this case.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons can be shared across many computations even without a neuron-count bottleneck, driven by regularization rather than capacity (a computation analogue of V3).

fits_no_version.finding: Freezing the first layer at random uniform values yields a similar readout pattern (Fig. 7). Binary weights improve loss only by a constant factor (Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Boolean functions of sparse features can be linearly read out from random superposed embeddings, with error.

record.problems: The study uses a deliberately simplified toy task with monosemantic inputs and outputs. The authors say they did not perform a full sparsity sweep, do not explain why the observed weight values are selected, and rely on approximate analysis that is not rigorously proved. Several reported comparisons are qualitative.
record.rows_left_out: No findings were left out. The paper's figures show further weight charts and similarity measurements, but these do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Storage of sparse features as nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, the sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry. Inputs here are monosemantic and not compressed.
Whether competition for capacity among features of differing importance yields dedicated versus shared dimensions. Output importance is equalized by design.
Whether polysemantic neurons in feature representation arise without capacity pressure. The dense-even-at-full-capacity observation concerns computation and is stated without data.
Feature distribution across neurons in LLMs and SAE recovery of sparse features.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional or multi-dimensional.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T6/discusses judgment is kept. The closest brush with a version is the claim that dense sharing persists at d = m choose 2, which would bear on V3 if it concerned feature representation and were backed by data. It concerns computation and no number is reported, so it is logged under fits_no_version. The loss-versus-d result (Fig. 2) and binary-similarity sweeps (Fig. 9) are unrecorded, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Feature storage as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether feature competition for representational capacity causes neuron polysemanticity or dedicated dimensions for important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Feature distribution in LLMs and feature recovery with dictionaries or SAEs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP (Universal-AND toy model)
rows.value: The model generally tends towards binary weights, taking on only two different values; the paper describes the circuit as dense, with a significant weight for every input at every neuron.
rows.note: A result about computational circuitry, not feature-storage directions.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP (Universal-AND toy model)
rows.size_stated: m = 100; d varies, including values much smaller than m²
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated whether trained models solve the Universal-AND task.

conditions.value: various values, including extremely low d

rows.value: The models find solutions capable of solving the Universal-AND problem, including at extremely low d.
rows.note: The paper does not give a numeric success rate here.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP (Universal-AND toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the learned circuit at higher input sparsity.
rows.value: The model starts to prefer more degenerate solutions, including pure-additive circuits roughly corresponding to zᵢₘ₊ⱼ = 0.4(vᵢ + vⱼ).
rows.note: The paper reports this as one of the outcomes at higher sparsity.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP (Universal-AND toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected whether compute-layer weights updated during training.
rows.value: Some models fail to update Wᵢⱼ from the initial values and rely entirely on readout weights.
rows.note: Reported as an alternative degenerate outcome; no frequency is stated.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP (Universal-AND toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected neuron input weights and readout weights.
rows.value: The Binary Weighted Circuit does not form; the readout chart has a lack of class C neurons and a more uniform distribution of weights.
rows.note: The outcome is described in the text accompanying the figure.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP (Universal-AND toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Compared readout patterns with the first-layer weights frozen at random values.
rows.value: A similar pattern of readouts results.
rows.note: The paper states the qualitative comparison; the plotted values are not transcribed in the text.
